lead: Potentiometry measures a cell EMF while almost no current flows, so the reading follows the Nernst equation and gives the concentration of an ion. Conductance measures how easily a solution carries current, which depends on the number and mobility of ions. Together they find endpoints without an indicator and check electrolyte strength. A pH meter in a water plant is potentiometry; a laboratory conductivity meter checking distilled water or battery acid is conductometry. The cells, formulas and titration curves below make both methods reliable.
prereq: You need: cells and electrode potentials from 4.1, the Nernst equation from 4.2, and reference electrodes from 4.3; basic resistance from school physics.

sections.h3: Potentiometry: EMF at almost zero current

blocks.text: Potentiometry finds concentration from the EMF of a cell when current is nearly zero. The cell has a reference electrode of fixed known potential and an indicator electrode that responds to the analyte. A high-impedance voltmeter, with input resistance near 10¹² Ω, measures the EMF. Almost no current flows, so the solution composition stays unchanged and the Nernst equation applies.

blocks.where: Ecell is the measured cell EMF in volts; Eindicator is the potential of the indicator electrode in volts; Ereference is the fixed potential of the reference electrode in volts. The sign reverses if the meter leads are reversed.

blocks.text: For a glass pH electrode the cell EMF changes by about 59 mV per pH unit at 25 °C. That is why a pH meter must be calibrated with buffer solutions of known pH.

items: Put a known volume of analyte in a beaker with the indicator and reference electrodes.
Fill the burette with titrant and stir gently.
Add titrant in small portions and record the stable EMF after each addition.
Take the endpoint at the steepest part of the jump, where ΔE/ΔV is largest, and read the volume.

blocks.text: Acid-base titrations use a glass pH electrode. Redox titrations use an inert platinum indicator electrode. Precipitation titrations, such as chloride with silver nitrate, use a silver indicator electrode. The method works for coloured or turbid solutions where an indicator dye would be hard to see.

Conductance is the ease with which a solution carries current. Resistance R is measured with an AC bridge, not DC, because DC would polarise the electrodes and change the solution near them. The cell constant l/A corrects for the geometry of the conductivity cell.

blocks.where: κ is specific conductance in S cm⁻¹; l is the distance between electrodes in cm; A is the electrode area in cm²; R is resistance in Ω; G = 1/R is conductance in S; l/A is the cell constant in cm⁻¹.

blocks.text: Specific conductance κ is the conductance of a 1 cm cube of solution. Its unit is S cm⁻¹. The cell constant l/A is found by measuring R for a standard KCl solution of known κ.

blocks.where: Λm is molar conductance in S cm² mol⁻¹; κ is specific conductance in S cm⁻¹; M is concentration in mol L⁻¹; 1000 converts litres to cm³.

blocks.text: Equivalent conductance Λeq uses normality N in eq L⁻¹: Λeq = 1000κ/N. Strong electrolytes are fully ionised. Their molar conductance rises only slightly on dilution and levels off at Λm∞. Weak electrolytes are partly ionised; dilution increases the degree of ionisation, so Λm rises sharply towards Λm∞. Kohlrausch law gives the limiting value from independent ions: Λm∞ = ν₊λ₊∞ + ν₋λ₋∞. Here ν₊ and ν₋ are the numbers of cations and anions per formula unit, and λ₊∞ and λ₋∞ are their ionic conductances at infinite dilution.

Conductance increases with temperature and depends on the nature of the ions. H⁺ and OH⁻ have unusually high mobilities in water, so acids and bases conduct much better than salts of similar concentration.

A conductometric titration follows conductance as titrant is added. Some syllabi call this conductometry. No indicator is needed. The endpoint is the intersection of the straight-line parts of the curve.

For HCl titrated with NaOH, before the endpoint H⁺ ions of high mobility are replaced by Na⁺ ions of lower mobility. Conductance falls in a straight line. At the equivalence volume only NaCl remains, so conductance is minimum. After the endpoint, excess Na⁺ and OH⁻ are added; OH⁻ has high mobility, so conductance rises. The curve is a V with the minimum at the endpoint.

For a weak acid titrated with a strong base, the weak acid is poorly ionised. Adding NaOH forms a fully ionised salt, so conductance rises before the endpoint. After the endpoint, excess OH⁻ gives a steeper rise. The endpoint is the intersection of the two straight lines, not a minimum.

The same method detects precipitation and redox endpoints when the ions or ionic species change. It is common in water analysis, quality control of battery acid, and checking distilled water purity. Compare potentiometry: there the endpoint is a sharp EMF jump; here it is a change of slope in conductance.

figure.caption: Conductance falls linearly as H⁺ is replaced by Na⁺, reaches a minimum at 25.0 mL, and rises as excess OH⁻ appears.

spec.aria: Conductance falls linearly to a minimum at 25 mL of sodium hydroxide and then rises, the V-shape of a strong acid-strong base conductometric titration.

examples.question: 25.0 mL of hydrochloric acid is titrated conductometrically with 0.100 M NaOH. The conductance is minimum at 25.0 mL. Find the concentration of HCl.
steps: Write the data: volume of HCl = 25.0 mL = 0.0250 L; concentration of NaOH = 0.100 M; volume of NaOH at the minimum = 25.0 mL = 0.0250 L.
Moles of NaOH = concentration × volume = 0.100 mol L⁻¹ × 0.0250 L = 0.00250 mol.
The reaction is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. It is 1:1, so moles of HCl = 0.00250 mol.
Concentration of HCl = moles / volume = 0.00250 mol / 0.0250 L = 0.100 M.
examples.answer: The concentration of HCl is 0.100 M.
examples.check:
v_hcl_ml = 25.0
c_naoh = 0.100
v_naoh_ml = 25.0
n_naoh = c_naoh * v_naoh_ml / 1000.0
n_hcl = n_naoh
c_hcl = n_hcl / (v_hcl_ml / 1000.0)
print(f"{n_naoh:.5f}")
print(f"{c_hcl:.3f}")

traps: Do not take the minimum as the endpoint for every conductometric titration. For a weak acid with a strong base, use the intersection of the straight-line branches.
A potentiometric EMF must be measured at near-zero current. A low-impedance meter draws current and shifts the reading.
In Λm = 1000κ/M, κ must be in S cm⁻¹ and M in mol L⁻¹; a concentration given in mol m⁻³ makes the answer 1000 times too small, and R must first be converted to κ = (l/A)/R.
The potentiometric endpoint is the steepest slope, maximum ΔE/ΔV, not the first or last reading of the jump.
Conductance includes every ion present. After the endpoint the excess titrant, not the analyte, controls the slope.

quiz.q: Define specific conductance and give its unit.
quiz.a: Specific conductance κ is the conductance of a 1 cm cube of solution; its unit is S cm⁻¹.

quiz.q: Why does a potentiometric measurement use a high-impedance voltmeter?
quiz.a: It keeps current near zero, avoids polarisation, and leaves the solution composition unchanged so the Nernst equation applies.

quiz.q: 20.0 mL of HCl needs 20.0 mL of 0.0500 M NaOH to reach the conductometric minimum. Find the HCl concentration.
quiz.a: Moles NaOH = 0.0500 × 0.0200 = 0.00100 mol. The reaction is 1:1, so moles HCl = 0.00100 mol. Concentration HCl = 0.00100 / 0.0200 = 0.0500 M.

quiz.q: A conductivity cell has cell constant 0.50 cm⁻¹ and resistance 40 Ω. Find κ.
Explain why conductance falls before and rises after the endpoint in an HCl + NaOH titration.
quiz.a: Before the endpoint, high-mobility H⁺ is replaced by lower-mobility Na⁺, so conductance falls. After the endpoint, excess OH⁻ has high mobility, so conductance rises.

quiz.q: A conductometric curve for a weak acid with a strong base has no minimum. How do you find the endpoint?
quiz.a: Extend the two straight-line branches before and after the equivalence point; their intersection gives the endpoint volume.

quiz.q: State Kohlrausch law for molar conductance at infinite dilution.
quiz.a: Λ<sub>m</sub>∞ = ν₊λ₊∞ + ν₋λ₋∞, where ν₊ and ν₋ are ion counts per formula unit and λ∞ values are ionic conductances at infinite dilution.

beyond: Not for the exam. Potentiometry is the basis of pH meters, ion-selective electrodes and automatic titrators in water treatment and pharmaceutical quality control. Conductance detectors are used in ion chromatography and in flow systems that watch water purity. Research moves these measurements onto chip-scale sensors and into battery management systems that track electrolyte condition. Search for ion-selective electrodes, conductometric detection and cell-constant calibration.
